UNIT 2 · STRATEGY VISIONING & SUCCESS IN PRACTICE (SiP)
Module 2 · Direction · Unit 2

UNIT INTENT
Unit overview (facilitator file): This unit helps leaders to determine the organisation’s strategy architecture, articulate its strategic intent and define the Success in Practice (SiP) of the chosen Strategy Intent.

Before the organisation can define where it is going, leaders must agree on what strategy actually means, in the precise, strategic sense, translated to operational reality, that makes every subsequent decision coherent.

Three connected outputs carry the unit: the Strategy Architecture, the Strategy Intent Statement and Success in Practice.

WHAT THE UNIT PRODUCES:
Each group builds three connected outputs, in this order.
1. The Strategy Architecture: the integrated strategic logic constructed from the 14 elements of the Strategy2Results® definition of strategy.
2. The Strategy Intent Statement: one crisp statement of strategic ambition derived from WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN.
3. Success in Practice (SiP): four confirmed statements, one for each SiP domain, read together as one picture of success.
The Architecture provides the logic. The Intent crystallises the ambition. Success in Practice makes the ambition observable.

HOW THE UNIT RUNS:
1. You teach the whole unit from this deck first, from Section 1 to the Unit Summary. The deck is the teaching material.
2. Participants then go to the portal and complete their own page, in the session or after it: the opening definition of strategy, the reflections and the group work of Section 5.
3. Section 4 is one worked example, Kestrel Point Services, read on the portal and taught from the deck.
4. Section 5 on the portal is group work for the Capstone. The group builds its own simulated company's Strategy Architecture, Strategy Intent Statement and Success in Practice. The group chooses its scribe for this work; the scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member's page. Each member then selects Agree.

Each slide's notes end with a block headed "On the portal, after the teaching" wherever participants have something to complete for that part.

Your preparation as facilitator:
- Read the Facilitator Guide tab and every section of the facilitator file.

Where the outputs go next:
- When every member has agreed, the three outputs feed the team's Capstone S2R Blueprint, parts 2A and 2B.

slides.title: Section 1 · Awareness — What
slides.notes:
SECTION 1 · AWARENESS — WHAT

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Frame strategic direction in terms of the value and success the organisation intends to create.
2. Differentiate strategic direction from the future position it seeks while maintaining coherence between them.


SECTION INTENT: This section establishes the conceptual bedrock of the entire unit. 
Before any co-creation can happen, participants must share a single, precise definition of strategy and understand its three building blocks: the Strategy Architecture, the Strategy Intent Statement and Success in Practice.

slides.title: Opening the session
slides.notes:
OPENING THE SESSION

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Ask for the definition.
Before showing any content, put this slide up and ask each participant to define strategy in their own words.
Say: "Write your definition of strategy in one sentence — right now, without consulting anyone."
Participants write on paper, without conferring.

2. Collect three or four responses.
Ask three or four participants to read their sentence aloud, word for word. Ask them to paste in the chat.

3. Ask the room what it hears.
Ask: "What do these definitions have in common? Where do they differ?"

Listen for: definitions that describe a plan ("the steps we take to…"), definitions that stop at ambition ("where we want to be in five years"), and definitions with no mention of value, stakeholders or the operating environment.
Hold back from correcting any definition. 

4. Name what you see.
Say: "Some of our definitions describe a plan. Some describe an ambition. Some describe a competitive intention."

5. Use the gap as the opening provocation.
Say: "This gap between our answers is exactly the problem this unit solves. This unit gives us one precise definition of strategy and the architecture that sits underneath it."

6. Keep the definitions.
Say: "Keep your sentence. We return to it at the Unit Summary."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Each participant enters their definition of strategy in the box at the top of Section 1 of the participant file: "Opening the Session — Your Definition of Strategy".

slides.title: 1.1a · Define the Strategy Architecture
slides.notes:
1.1 — DEFINE THE STRATEGY ARCHITECTURE (9 CONCEPTS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Link to the opening exercise.
Say: "We have just heard several definitions of strategy in this room. 
Strategy is frequently used but rarely precisely defined. 
In most organisations it functions as shorthand for ambition, planning, or competitive intention, with each executive leader carrying a slightly different version of the word. 
In the Strategy2Results® framework, strategy has a specific applied definition - the interconnected choices and logic that determine what the organisation does, we call this the Strategy Architecture.
Every strategy for any organisations takes complexity, uncertainty and gives it structure.

2. Read the definition.
Say: "We are now going to unpack the Strategy2Results® definition of strategy."
Read the definition on the slide aloud once, slowly:

"Strategy is the output of iterative thinking, logic and process to determine what, why, how and when an organisation creates, delivers and sustains value to its stakeholders while navigating the forces within its operating environment."

Ask one participant to read it a second time.

Then say: "Every word in this definition carries strategic weight, hence I said we are giving you an applied definition of strategy."

3. Compare it with the definitions of the room.
Ask: "Which words in this definition are missing from ours?"
Take two or three answers. Listen for: value, stakeholders, the forces, the operating environment. 
These are the words most opening definitions leave out.

4. Name the parts.
Ask: how many components we have in our applied definition?
Point to each part of the definition as you name it: the output · iterative thinking, logic and process · what, why, how and when · creates, delivers and sustains value · stakeholders · navigating the forces · the operating environment.

Say: "Each concept in the definition represents part of the strategy architecture."

5. Leave one question with the group.
Say: "As we work through the concepts, consider: How well defined is each part of your current organisational strategy architecture?"

6. Bridge to the next slide.
Say: "Once we understand the parts and how they connect, we can begin constructing a coherent strategic position. 
For each concept we look at three things: what it means, what it implies for execution, and what breaks when it is absent."

slides.title: 1.1 · Building the Strategy Architecture
slides.notes:
1.1 — DEFINE THE STRATEGY ARCHITECTURE · THE NINE CONCEPTS

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open.
Say: "We take the nine concepts one at a time. For each one: what it means, its strategic implication, and what fails when it is missing."

2. OUTPUT — A decided position.

What it means, say: "Strategy is a tangible, expressible, decided position. The output is what can be tested, challenged, and acted upon."

Strategic implication, say: "Clarity of direction. People know what the organisation has committed to and can align decisions to it."

Failure if missing, say: "Strategy remains trapped in conversations. Activity is mistaken for direction. 
No one can articulate what was actually decided."

EXAMPLE“Over the next three years, we will grow our corporate banking business by becoming the primary transaction-banking partner for mid-sized enterprises in Southern Africa, prioritising digital transaction services and existing-market expansion.”
This works because it is expressible and testable. 
Leadership can challenge it: Why this customer? Why transaction banking? Why these markets? And functions can begin aligning decisions, resources and priorities around it.

You could then contrast it briefly:
Not an output: “We held a strategy retreat and agreed that growth and digitalisation are priorities.”

A decided position: “We will grow through X, for Y customer, in Z arena, by making these choices.”

Add: "The decided position is distinct from a plan, a meeting, the process of strategising, the presentation deck, and the off-site discussion."

3. ITERATIVE —

What it means, say: "Strategy is never finished in one pass. It is a hypothesis that loops: form, test against reality, revise, repeat."

Strategic implication, say: "Adaptability. The organisation stays responsive to changing conditions without losing its overall direction."

Failure if missing, say: "Strategy becomes doctrine — defended as settled belief and closed to evidence. 
Stale assumptions compound until the organisation is blindsided.“

EXAMPLE
Kodak’s strategy was built around a world in which photographic film remained central to how people captured and preserved images. 
Ironically, Kodak itself developed one of the first digital cameras in 1975. 
The signals that photography was moving towards digital were therefore not entirely external to the company.
Its established strategic logic remained influential for too long while the environment was changing around it.
The strategic hypothesis needed to be repeatedly tested: Is film still where value will be created? 
How is customer behaviour changing? What business are we becoming as photography becomes digital?

Add: "This rules out strategy as an annual ritual and rules in strategy as a living organisational capability.“

4. THINKING & LOGIC — The cognitive engine.

What it means, say: "Thinking is divergent and exploratory — generating hypotheses and questioning assumptions. 
Logic is convergent and analytical — testing what must be true for the strategy to hold. Both are required in sequence."

Strategic implication, say: "Strategy is reasoned. This prevents both wishful thinking and paralysis by analysis."

Failure if missing, say: "Either wishful vision (thinking without logic) or analysis paralysis (logic without fresh thinking). 
Most organisations over-invest in data and under-invest in genuinely uncomfortable questions."

Deepen, say: "People misread what is in front of them when they are held by old assumptions. 
Leaders who are too attached to what they already believe can miss the very signal that could renew the organisation."
(Insight: Rigid mental models. Source: Journal, 3 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

Add: "Strategy needs reasoning as well as inspiration."

5. PROCESS — The structured container.

What it means, say: "Process converts ad hoc thinking into a repeatable, auditable, scalable method. 
It defines who is involved, what inputs are needed, which tools are used, and what decisions are made at each stage.“

Strategic implication, say: "Strategy becomes an organisational capability. 
It survives leadership change and does not restart from zero each cycle.“

Failure if missing, say: "Strategy is brilliant but fragile. When the individual who carries it in their head leaves, the capability collapses."

Deepen, say: "When value becomes inseparable from particular individuals, ego and fragility increase. 
Strong cultures recognise the contribution while keeping the mission larger than the contributor."
(Insight: The mission larger than the contributor. Source: Journal, 18 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

Add: "With process, strategy stops being a personality-dependent event. Process is the scaffolding that makes thinking transferable."

Linger on Thinking & Logic and Process.
Say: "Thinking & Logic is the cognitive engine. Process is the structured container. 
Most organisations have process but neglect thinking quality. The definition forces us to see this gap."
Ask: "Where does your organisation invest more: in the quality of the thinking, or in the process that contains it?"
Take two or three answers. Listen for: a strategy process with no named place for uncomfortable questions.

6. WHAT · WHY · HOW · WHEN — The 3Ws & H — complete decision space.

What it means, say: "These four dimensions define every coherent strategy. 
WHAT sets the ambition and scope. 
WHY establishes the differentiating logic or purpose. 
HOW defines the operating model. 
WHEN governs timing and sequencing.“

Strategic implication, say: "A complete and internally consistent strategy. 
Each dimension is a necessary condition for the others."

Failure if missing, say: "Structural incompleteness.
WHAT and WHY without HOW and WHEN is vision without execution. 

You ask this - 

What does HOW without WHY produce?
 is activity without purpose.“

What does WHEN without WHAT produce?
is urgency without direction

Add: "Together the four dimensions constitute a complete strategic position."

7. CREATES · DELIVERS · SUSTAINS — The Value Triad.

What it means, say: "Creating value means nothing if it does not reach its intended recipients. 
Delivering value means nothing if the conditions that make it possible are steadily depleted. 
All three layers must be explicitly designed and invested in.“

Strategic implication, say: "Long-term viability. The organisation does not harvest today at the expense of tomorrow. 
Value compounds over time.“

Failure if missing, say: "Most organisations over-invest in creation and delivery while underinvesting in sustainability — the culture, financial health, and ecosystem relationships that make value durable.“

8. STAKEHOLDERS — Broader than customers.

What it means, say: "Everyone with a stake in the organisation's actions:
Ask who are these - Listen for: stakeholders answered as "customers". Ask: "Who else has a stake in what this organisation does?"
customers, employees, investors, communities, regulators, and partners. 
The choice of this word is a values statement — strategy must account for the full stakeholder universe.“

Strategic implication, say: "Legitimacy and resilience. Organisations that optimise for one stakeholder class create fragilities that others eventually exploit or oppose.“

Failure if missing, say: "Blind spots. When any stakeholder group is systematically ignored, each becomes a structural risk."

An organisation can have alignment, resources, skill and momentum and still fail when its strategy rests on the wrong foundation. 
A strategy designed mainly to build the reputation of its builders serves the wrong master. 
Anchor strategy in what the organisation is trying to achieve for its stakeholders."
(Insight: Value for whom. Source: Journal, 10 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

Add: "The blind spots are specific: employees who deliver value, investors who fund it, regulators who permit it."

9. NAVIGATING — Active, skilful movement through forces.

What it means, say: "Navigation implies agency — the deliberate, skilled reading of forces and the intentional choice of how to move in response to them. 
Strategy is a continuous navigation discipline: the forces in the operating environment do not pause when the strategy is set, when targets are reached, or when the organisation is performing well.“

Strategic implication, say: "The organisation maintains strategic control even as conditions shift. 
Leaders make deliberate moves and shape their circumstances. 
Navigation transforms external pressure from a threat into a manageable variable.“

Failure if missing, say: "The organisation becomes reactive — responding to what has already happened, with little anticipation of what is coming. Reactive organisations lose strategic initiative and operate in permanent catch-up. 
Navigation is what separates strategic leadership from operational management."

10. THE FORCES — Five categories every strategy must navigate.

What it means, say: "Five distinct force categories continuously shape the environment in which strategy must deliver."
Name the five categories, one at a time:
1. Competitive forces: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, and shifts in customer power.
2. Macro-environmental forces: economic cycles, regulatory frameworks, political dynamics, and technological infrastructure.
3. Disruptive forces: new business models and technology applications emerging at the margins of the industry.
4. Social and environmental forces: stakeholder expectations, social norms, ESG standards, and demographic shifts operating simultaneously across all stakeholder groups.
5. Internal forces: culture, enterprise behaviour patterns, institutional habits, and legacy identity that exert force on the organisation from within, often in opposition to the stated strategy.

Strategic implication, say: "Leaders develop a structured awareness of which forces are most active, most rapidly shifting, and most likely to invalidate current strategic assumptions. 
Each force category requires a specific navigation discipline — and this programme builds those disciplines across its units.“

Failure if missing, say: "Strategy is designed for a force environment that no longer exists. 
The organisation discovers that the competitive, macro, disruptive, social, or internal forces have moved — and that the strategy has not. 
By the time this gap is visible in results, the cost of recalibration is significantly higher than it would have been with earlier navigation."

11. Bring the nine together.
Ask: "Which of these nine concepts is least visible in how your organisation currently talks about strategy?"
Take three or four answers and note them. They show where each group will need to work hardest in Section 5.

12. Bridge to 1.2.
Say: "OUTPUT is what the other concepts produce: the Strategy Architecture. 
In Section 4 you see this definition worked as 14 elements for one company, and in Section 5 your group works it for its own company." 

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the 1.1 reflection: "Which part of your organisation's strategy architecture is least well defined today? What is the consequence?"

slides.title: 1.2 · Defining the Strategy Intent Statement
slides.notes:
1.2 — DEFINING THE STRATEGY INTENT STATEMENT (4 DIMENSIONS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Position the statement.
Say: "The Strategy Architecture provides the foundation from which the Strategy Intent Statement is derived.
It has established the organisation's strategic choices and the logic connecting them.
The Strategy Intent Statement brings forward four dimensions from that architecture.“

Say: "The Strategy Architecture holds the depth and the supporting logic.
The Strategy Intent Statement is crisp, directional and easy to express.“

Tell participants: they derive their own statement in Section 5. Here they learn what it brings forward.

2. Say why the statement must be crisp.
Say: "A message creates value only if people can receive and understand it.
Strategy must be both sound and communicable."
(Insight: Sound and communicable. Source: Journal, 23 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

3. Take the four dimensions one at a time.
Say: "We walk through WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN one at a time, as a group."
For each dimension, ask one diagnostic question and take two or three responses.
Stay longest on HOW and WHEN: they typically reveal the most significant gaps.

4. WHAT — Scope & Definition.
Say: "WHAT brings forward the value the organisation has chosen to create and its field of play.
It governs scope, portfolio, product and service definition, boundary-setting, market choice, capability focus."

Ask one diagnostic question and take two or three responses: "What arenas are we choosing to compete in?" · "What have we decided not to do?" · Listen for: a WHAT with no boundary.

Deepen, say: "Capability without strategic intent produces a spectacular career and an unfinished assignment.
Audit where the organisation’s most distinctive strength is being spent.
(Insight: Capability without intent. Source: Journal, 25 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

5. WHY — Purpose & Rationale.
Say: "WHY brings forward the rationale for those choices and why they matter.
It governs purpose, mission, competitive differentiation, value proposition, organisational identity."

Ask one diagnostic question and take two or three responses: "Does our WHY actually differentiate us, or could a competitor claim it unchanged?" · "Do our decisions consistently reflect this WHY?" · "Do stakeholders believe and repeat our WHY?"

Deepen, say: "Organisations that rush into execution without clarifying purpose create activity without lasting impact.
Strategic clarity emerges when leaders understand why the work exists before deciding how it will be done."
(Insight: WHY before HOW. Source: Journal, 28 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

6. HOW — Mechanism & Model.
Say: "HOW brings forward the operating model, capabilities and mechanisms through which the value will be delivered.
It governs operating model, capabilities, processes, organisational design, technology architecture, partnerships."

Key facilitation moment. Ask: "Does your operating model currently match your strategy — or is it a legacy structure that predates your current direction?"

Stay here. This often opens the most honest conversation of the entire Awareness section.

Further diagnostic questions, if the room needs them: "What capabilities are core and must be owned versus outsourced?" ·
"Where are the HOW gaps between strategic ambition and current capability?"

Listen for: a HOW with no operating model, capability or mechanism named.

Deepen, say: "A common strategic failure is choosing the right goal and accepting a compromised route to reach it: a deal that delivers the number and burns the relationship, a hire that fits the seat and damages the team.

Before the next material commitment, write the destination and the route on two separate lines and ask whether you would still defend the route if the outcome failed."
(Insight: Destination and route. Source: Journal, 24 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

7. WHEN — Timing & Sequencing.
Say: "WHEN brings forward the timing, sequencing and strategic moves through which the ambition will be pursued.
It governs timing, sequencing, pacing, prioritisation, horizon planning, entry and exit decisions."

Ask: "Have you actually mapped the sequence of moves needed to achieve your strategy — or does the plan treat all initiatives as running in parallel?"

Further diagnostic questions, if the room needs them: "Are we moving at the right pace?" · "What signals tell us when to accelerate or pause?"

Deepen, say: "Many strategic failures are failures of timing.
The leader knew what to do and moved before the conditions favoured it. Identify one important move you are pushing early because you are anxious to resolve uncertainty.
The same move made at the right moment is a different move."
(Insight: Timing failures. Source: Journal, 1 May 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

8. Read the room.
Ask: "Which of the four dimensions is least clearly defined in your organisation today?"
Take a show of hands for each dimension and say what pattern the group shows.

9. Show that the four hold together.
Say: "The four dimensions are interdependent. Answering only two or three creates a structurally incomplete strategy.
A well-formed strategic intent answers all four at once: What value are we creating?
Why will stakeholders choose us?
How will we deliver this value?
When will we act?"

10. Say what is at stake.
Say: "Without a clear strategic intent, every investment becomes a negotiation without a shared reference point.
Every performance review becomes a contest between competing definitions of success."

11. Close and bridge to 1.3.
Say: "These four dimensions are then crystallised into one clear Strategy Intent Statement.
The strength of the statement comes from the architecture beneath it.
It should therefore be crisp, directional and easy to express, while the Strategy Architecture holds the depth and supporting logic.
The resulting Strategy Intent becomes the organisation's directional anchor for strategic choices, alignment and execution."

Say: "The Intent sets the ambition. Next we ask what we should see in practice when that ambition is realised."

slides.title: 1.3 · Defining the Success in Practice
slides.notes:
1.3 — SUCCESS IN PRACTICE (SiP): FROM INTENT TO FUTURE REALITY (4 OBSERVABLE DOMAINS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Connect the two outputs.
Say: "The Strategy Intent Statement establishes the ambition. 
Success in Practice defines what must be seen, experienced and executed for that ambition to become reality within a given time horizon."

Add: "Once the organisation has answered WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN, the next step is to translate that clarity into an observable future reality."

2. Say what Success in Practice is.
Say: "Success in Practice, SiP, translates strategic intent into a clear picture of the future operating reality of the organisation.
It answers a question that most strategy processes fail to address clearly."
Read the central question from the foot of the slide:
"If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"

3. Position participants inside the future.
Say: "For this first look, use the strategic ambition of your own organisation as it stands today. Assume the strategy has worked. From here, we are observing."
Ask participants to describe the observable organisational reality. Each group writes its own Strategy Intent Statement in Section 5.

4. Take the four indicators.
Say: "Success is considered across four observable indicators

Name each indicator from the slide and say what it covers:

- D1 · Customer Experience & Value: What customers and other value recipients experience when the strategic intent is working.

- D2 · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm: How the organisation operates, coordinates, delivers and adapts when the capabilities required by the intent are functioning effectively.

- D3 · People & Culture Dynamics: How people understand the strategic intent, make decisions, collaborate, take ownership and behave when the intent is embedded in the organisation.

- D4 · Enterprise Value Creation: How the organisation benefits across its measures of enterprise success.

Take one observation from the room for each indicator, D1 to D4.

Add: "Anchoring the description in four observable indicators keeps us out of vague storytelling."

5. Keep the room on observable reality.
Say: "The SiP describes what is happening when the strategy is working. Initiatives, projects and activities stay out of it.“

6. Say why success is defined before anything is built.
Say: "Before you build, know exactly what you are building towards and why each element matters."

(Insight: Built to a specification. Source: Journal, 15 February 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

7. Say what a shared picture gives a leadership team.
Say: "Defining this together creates a shared picture of success, reducing the risk of different functions interpreting the same strategic intent differently."

Say: "The aim is shared construction: we should leave with a common understanding of what success looks like across the organisation."

Name the four effects for an executive team:
- It removes ambiguity about what the strategy is actually aiming to produce.
- It creates a shared mental model of the future state across all functions.
- It provides a decision filter: every initiative, investment and priority can be tested against it.
- It enables recognition of progress: leaders can see alignment and momentum during execution.

8. Close and bridge.
Say: "Together, the four indicators create a shared organisational picture of success against which decisions, trade-offs and execution can be aligned."

slides.title: Section 1 Reflection · Awareness
slides.notes:
SECTION 1 REFLECTION

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the question aloud.
Reflection — Awareness: "Which part of your organisation’s or team’s strategy architecture is least defined, and how would you define it?"

2. Say what the reflection is for.
Point learners to the portal section that they will be required to complete with as much depth as possible.
The reflections build the learning portfolio they receive at the end of the programme. Each one carries 20 of the 100 marks for the unit.

Say: "You write this reflection on the portal after the teaching, with as much depth as you can."

3. Set the standard.
Tell learners what a full answer does: Names the specific element that is least defined and sets out how they would define it for their own context.

Deepen, say: "Strategy begins with an accurate understanding of present reality.
Leaders who avoid difficult information protect their comfort at the expense of the institution.
Name the true condition without minimising it."
(Insight: An honest baseline. Source: Journal, 4 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

4. Bridge to Section 2.
Say: "We now have the three building blocks: the architecture, the intent and the picture of success.

Section 2 asks why the Strategy Intent and SiP matter once they are defined."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the reflection in Section 1 of the participant file.

slides.title: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
slides.notes:
SECTION 2 · INTELLIGENCE — WHY

HOW THIS SECTION RUNS:
1. 2.1 overview: the three functions the Strategy Intent and SiP serve within the Strategy2Results® architecture.
2. 2.1.1 Strategic Alignment, 2.1.2 Decision Filter and 2.1.3 Execution Coherence: one slide each. Every function is taught in three parts: Why It Matters, what the Strategy Intent does, and what SiP does.
3. The Section 2 Reflections slide: the reflection participants write on the portal after the teaching.

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. Link from Section 1.
Say: "Section 1 defined the three building blocks. This section asks what the Strategy Intent and SiP do for a leadership team once they exist.“

2. Read the two section learning outcomes from the slide.
SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Reconcile leadership perspectives into a shared strategic ambition and picture of success.
2. Apply strategic direction as a consistent basis for enterprise decisions.

3. State the section intent.
Say: "The Strategy Intent and SiP become useful when they begin to shape how the organisation aligns, makes choices and executes."
Say: "Once leaders have established a shared strategic ambition and defined what success looks like in practice, those two outputs become common reference points across the organisation."

4. Bridge to 2.1.
Say: "The Strategy Intent and SiP serve three important functions. The next slide names them."

slides.title: 2.1 · Intent & SiP in the S2R® Architecture
slides.notes:
2.1 — ROLE OF STRATEGY INTENT & SiP IN THE S2R® ARCHITECTURE (3 FUNCTIONS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Introduce the three functions.
Say: "Strategy Intent and SiP serve three functions within the Strategy2Results® architecture."

Name each function from the slide:

- Strategic Alignment: keeping people and functions oriented around the same ambition and picture of success.

- Decision Filter: providing a basis for determining which choices, opportunities and investments support the strategy.

- Execution Coherence: helping different functions understand how their individual contributions must connect to produce the enterprise outcome.

2. Name the pairing that runs through all three.
Say: "The Intent anchors the ambition and strategic choices; SiP anchors the organisational reality those choices are intended to produce."
"The two outputs are there to govern alignment, choices and execution."

3. Leave one question with the group.
Say: "As we move through the three functions, consider: What happens in an organisation when this function is weak or absent?"

4. Bridge to the next slide.
Say: "The next three slides take one function each: why it matters, what the Strategy Intent does, and what SiP does."

slides.title: 2.1.1 · Strategic Alignment
slides.notes:
2.1.1 — STRATEGIC ALIGNMENT

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Say why it matters.
Say: "Strategy fragments when leaders and functions interpret the organisation's ambition differently. 
Alignment creates a common strategic reference point while allowing different parts of the organisation to make the contributions required of them."

2. Give the role of the Strategy Intent.
Say: "The Strategy Intent creates shared understanding of the organisation's strategic ambition and the choices that define it. 
Leaders are anchored to the same WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN."

Deepen, say: "Intent cannot be executed consistently when people do not know the principles, expectations and boundaries that should govern their decisions."
(Insight: Shared understanding. Source: Journal, 19 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

3. Give the role of SiP.
Say: "SiP creates a shared picture of what successful realisation of that ambition looks like. 
Functions may contribute differently, but they are working towards the same organisational reality.“

Deepen, say: "Culture becomes powerful when people who share an institution also share its meaning and act on it together."
(Insight: Shared meaning, shared action. Source: Journal, 15 July 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

4. Test alignment against the opening exercise.
Say: "When this session opened, we heard several definitions of strategy in one room."
Ask: "If each member of your leadership team described your organisation’s strategic ambition in one sentence, how many versions would you hear?"

5. Ask what happens when strategic alignment is weak.
Ask: "What happens in an organisation when strategic alignment is weak or absent?"
Listen for: leaders and functions interpreting the ambition differently; each executive pursuing a personal interpretation of the scope and its differentiating logic; each function describing its own version of the future operating state.

6. Bridge to the Decision Filter.
Say: "Alignment gives us one reference point. The next function puts that reference point to work on choices."

slides.title: 2.1.2 · Decision Filter
slides.notes:
2.1.2 — DECISION FILTER

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Say why it matters.
Say: "Organisations continuously face competing opportunities, investments, initiatives and demands. 
Without a common strategic filter, priorities can become shaped by urgency, functional interests or whoever has the strongest influence in the room."

Deepen, say: "Many legitimate demands fragment attention unless there is a clear organising priority. 
Effective strategy knows the “one thing” around which competing choices are ordered."
(Insight: The one thing. Source: Journal, 18 September 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

2. Make it practical.
Ask: "When a new initiative, investment or opportunity appears, what tells us whether it belongs in our strategy?"
Take three answers before you give the two tests.

3. Give the two tests on the slide.
Say: "The Strategy Intent provides the test of strategic fit. 
SiP provides the test of strategic contribution: whether the choice moves the organisation closer to the success it has defined."

The test of strategic fit:
Say: "The Strategy Intent provides the reference point for determining whether a choice is consistent with the organisation's strategic ambition and the choices already made."

The test of strategic contribution:
Say: "SiP tests whether that choice contributes to the conditions of success the organisation has defined. It connects individual decisions to the future reality they are expected to help create."

4. Run both tests on a real case.
Ask one participant to name a real initiative that is competing for resources in their organisation today. 
Run both tests aloud against that organisation’s current strategic ambition and its current picture of success.

Say: "Use the same two tests each time a new initiative, investment or opportunity appears."

5. Deepen: the filter is how daily decisions are made.
Say: "A strong strategy carries a clear operating logic that guides what is prioritised, how trade-offs are made and how consistency holds under pressure. Execution quality depends on how those decisions are made daily."
(Insight: Operating logic. Source: Journal, 3 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

6. Deepen: name the governing reference points.
Say: "Organisations without an explicit governing reference point drift into convergent decline: each person makes locally rational decisions that are collectively damaging."

7. Ask what happens when decision filter is weak.
Ask: "What happens in an organisation when decision filter is weak or absent?"

Listen for: priorities shaped by urgency, by functional interests, or by whoever has the strongest influence in the room; an initiative that passes the test of fit while nobody asks what it contributes to the defined success.

8. Bridge to Execution Coherence.
Say: "The filter governs single choices. The next function asks whether the work of all the functions adds up."

slides.title: 2.1.3 · Execution Coherence
slides.notes:
2.1.3 — EXECUTION COHERENCE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Say why it matters.
Say: "Strategy is delivered through many functions, teams and decisions acting together. 
Each part can perform well individually while the organisation still fails to produce the intended enterprise outcome. Coherence ensures those contributions connect."

2. Give the role of the Strategy Intent.
Say: "The Strategy Intent provides the common strategic anchor that enables functions to interpret their mandates and choices in relation to the enterprise ambition."

3. Give the role of SiP.
Say: "SiP shows what those combined contributions must produce across customer value, operational capability, people and culture, and enterprise value. 
It allows functions to see beyond their individual outputs to the organisational outcome they collectively enable."

4. Make it real.
Ask: "Where in your organisation does every function meet its own targets while the enterprise outcome falls short?"
Take two or three answers.

5. Deepen.
Say: "Organisations that want to keep their core commitments coherent must resist fragmenting the practice of those commitments into locally adapted, individually customised forms that gradually lose their connection to the common centre."
(Insight: The common centre. Source: Journal, 24 March 2026 — Professional Insights)

6. Ask what happens when execution coherence is weak.
Ask: "What happens in an organisation when execution coherence is weak or absent?"

Listen for: each function performing well against its own measures while the enterprise outcome is missed; functions losing sight of the organisational outcome they collectively enable; contributions that do not connect at the boundaries between functions.

7. Point forward and bridge.
Say: "Section 5 puts this function to work: your group builds one Strategy Intent and one Success in Practice that every function in your company can read its contribution against."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the 2.1 reflection: "Which of the three functions is weakest in your organisation today? What happens as a result?"

slides.notes:

4. Bridge to Section 3.

slides.title: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 · EXTRAPOLATING — WHERE

HOW TO OPEN THE SECTION:

1. State the section intent.
Say: "We have established that Success in Practice answers a central question: If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice? This section takes that question deeper."

SECTION LEARNING OUTCOMES:
1. Specify observable evidence of success across the four SiP domains.
2. Interpret gaps between intended success and current conditions to identify strategic misalignment.

2. Say why broad statements fall short.
Say: "Each of the four SiP domains covers an important part of organisational reality.
Leaders need to be able to recognise what success would actually look like when it begins to show up in practice."

3. Introduce the observable indicators.
Say: "This is where observable indicators become useful. 
The indicators help us examine each SiP domain more deeply. 
They show the kinds of conditions we would expect to observe when that aspect of the Strategy Intent is working, as well as the signals that may indicate something is missing."

4. Introduce the second discipline: balance.
Say: "There is also a second discipline: balance across the four domains. 
A leadership team can develop a strong picture of customer success while overlooking the operational capability required to deliver it. 
It can describe an enabling culture without connecting that culture to enterprise value. 
It can define strong financial outcomes without describing the customer, operational and people conditions required to produce them."

5. Name the two disciplines.
Say: "This section therefore develops two disciplines: Depth within each SiP domain. Balance across all four SiP domains."
Tell participants: both disciplines return in 4.3, where the worked example applies them, and in Section 5, where each group tests its own Success in Practice.

7. Say how the section runs.
Say: "We begin by examining the observable indicators within each domain. 
We then examine what happens when one domain becomes dominant and begins to distort the organisation's overall picture of success."

slides.title: 3.1a · SiP Observable Indicators
slides.notes:
3.1 — SiP OBSERVABLE INDICATORS (4 DOMAINS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Say what an observable indicator is for.
Say: "Each SiP domain is examined through a set of observable indicators. 
These indicators help leaders move from a broad description of success to the specific conditions through which that success would become visible in the organisation."

2. Explain the two positions.
Say: "For every indicator, we examine two positions."
Say: "When Working describes what we would expect to observe when that aspect of the SiP is functioning effectively."
Say: "Signal of Absence describes what may become visible when that condition is weak, missing or disconnected from the Strategy Intent."

3. Say how the two positions are used.
Say: "Use both positions to deepen the discussion. Sometimes the absence of a condition provides the clearest evidence of why it matters."

4. Place the indicators correctly.
Say: "The indicators sit alongside the organisation's SiP. 
They help leaders test, deepen and make observable the success they have defined."

5. Name the four domains and their indicators.
The slide shows the indicators in short form. Give the full names:

- D1 · Customer Experience & Value: C — Connection Value · A — Access Value · R — Results Value · E — Effort Value

- D2 · Operational Capability: Priority Clarity · Decision Flow · Cross-Functional Coordination · Delivery Rhythm

- D3 · People & Culture: Cross-Boundary Collaboration · Ownership Culture · Strategic Alignment · Dialogue Quality

- D4 · Enterprise Value: Growth Trajectory · Profitability Quality · Market Position · Value Durability

Say: "No domain is a single metric."

6. Bridge to the next slide.
Say: "The next four slides take one domain each. For every indicator we look at When Working, then at the Signal of Absence."

slides.title: 3.1b · D1 Customer Experience & Value
slides.notes:
3.1 — SiP OBSERVABLE INDICATORS · D1 · CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE & VALUE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Introduce the domain.
Say: "This domain is Customer Experience & Value. 
Customers encounter the organisation through People, Processes, Products and Platforms, and experience four forms of value: the CARE Model."

Add: "Each of the four is the source of one form of value. People: Connection Value. Platforms: Access Value. Products: Results Value. Processes: Effort Value.“

For each domain, teach the positive indicator and ask for the results of the missing indicator.

2. C — Connection Value.
When Working, say: "Customers feel understood, respected, and supported. 
The people representing the organisation genuinely care about their problem."

Add: "Customers trust that the care extends beyond the transaction."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Customers describe interactions as transactional, impersonal, or difficult. They feel processed."

3. A — Access Value.
When Working, say: "Customers can interact quickly, easily, and reliably through their preferred channels.
Availability and responsiveness are consistent."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Customers describe friction, unavailability, or inconsistency. Digital and service channels feel designed for the organisation's convenience."

Deepen, say: "Organisations that want to serve their stakeholders consistently cannot leave that service to individual discretion. 
The most reliable provision is built into the institutional rhythm and does not depend on the surplus or the mood of the current leadership."
(Insight: Structured into the rhythm. Source: Journal, 25 March 2026 — Professional Insights)

4. R — Results Value.
When Working, say: "Customers receive solutions that actually solve their problems and improve their outcomes. 
Performance is reliable; the product does what it promises."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Customers report that the offering underdelivers against its stated value. 
Complaints cluster around gaps between promise and performance."

5. E — Effort Value.
When Working, say: "Customers experience simple, predictable processes that require minimal effort. 
Complexity is absorbed by the organisation."

Add: "No complexity is passed to the customer."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Customers describe the experience as complicated, slow, or requiring too many steps. 
They feel they are doing the organisation's job for it."

Stay longest here. Effort Value asks who carries the complexity: the customer or the organisation.

Ask: "Where does your customer carry effort or complexity that the organisation should absorb?"

6. Ask the room what it recognises.
Ask: "Which of the four forms of value would your customers say they receive from you most reliably? Which would they name last?"
Ask: "Which of these signals of absence do you already hear in your customers’ complaints?"

Take two or three answers. Keep the discussion on what can be observed: what a customer, an employee or a board member would see or hear.

7. Link the domain to Section 5.
Say: "In Section 5 your group writes one Customer Experience & Value statement. 
The lead question is: If the intent succeeds, what should customers and other value recipients see and experience? 
These indicators deepen that discussion. The statement itself stays focused on your own Strategy Intent."

8. Bridge to the next domain.
Say: "Next: D2, how the organisation operates and executes."

slides.title: 3.1c · D2 Operational Capability
slides.notes:
3.1 — SiP OBSERVABLE INDICATORS · D2 · OPERATIONAL CAPABILITY

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Introduce the domain.
Say: "This domain is Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm. 
It shows how the organisation operates internally when its strategy is translating into results. It is observable through four execution indicators."
The slide shows the When Working position of each indicator. 

2. Priority Clarity.
When Working, say: "Strategic priorities are explicit, stable, and understood across every function. 
Leaders can state the top priorities without checking a document — and their answers match."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Leaders describe different priorities. 
Resources are spread across too many initiatives. Every function has a different view of what matters most."

Ask: "Could each leader in your executive team or people in the organisation state the top priorities without checking a document? 
Would the answers match?"

3. Decision Flow.
When Working, say: "Decisions are made at the right level, with the right information, at the right speed. 
Authority is matched to accountability."

Add: "The organisation does not bottleneck at the top.“

Ask the difference between authority and accountability.

Say: Authority is the right to make decisions and direct action; accountability is the obligation to answer for the results of those decisions and actions.

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Decisions queue upward and slow down. 
Leaders feel they cannot act without approval. Strategic momentum is lost in governance process."

Add: "It is the leaders below CXO level who feel they cannot act without approval."

Ask: "Where do decisions queue in your organisation, and who is waiting for them?"

4. Cross-Functional Coordination.
When Working, say: "Hand-offs between functions are smooth, responsibilities are unambiguous, and execution friction is visible, named, and managed."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Teams work hard in their own lanes but create problems at the boundaries.
Hand-offs are where value leaks. White space between functions is ungoverned."

Add: "Execution friction that is silently absorbed goes unmanaged."
Ask: "Which hand-off between two functions leaks the most value today?"

5. Delivery Rhythm.
When Working, say: "Teams operate to a predictable cadence — weekly, monthly, quarterly — and delivery is consistent and reliable across the enterprise."

Add: "The cadence is weekly signal scanning, monthly performance reads, and quarterly strategic review."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Execution is reactive and event-driven. Reviews happen only when there is a crisis."

Add: "Review has not become a disciplined organisational habit, and delivery is variable and unpredictable."

Deepen, say: "Sustained organisational presence requires daily tending. 
Organisations that keep up the consistent daily act accumulate a depth of trust that occasional spectacular performance cannot replicate."
(Insight: Daily tending. Source: Journal, 23 February 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

6. Ask the room what it recognises.
Ask: "Which Signal of Absence in this domain do you recognise in your own organisation?"
Take two or three answers. Keep the discussion on what can be observed: what a customer, an employee or a board member would see or hear.

7. Link the domain to Section 5.
Say: "In Section 5 your group writes one Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm statement. 
The lead question is: If the intent succeeds, what should be visible in how the organisation operates and executes? 
These indicators deepen that discussion. The statement itself stays focused on your own Strategy Intent."

8. Bridge to the next domain.
Say: "Next: D3, how people understand, decide and behave."

slides.title: 3.1d · D3 People & Culture
slides.notes:
3.1 — SiP OBSERVABLE INDICATORS · D3 · PEOPLE & CULTURE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Introduce the domain.
Say: "This domain is People & Culture Dynamics. It shows the observable behavioural patterns when the organisation is at its best, when culture is actively reinforcing the strategic direction."

2. Cross-Boundary Collaboration.
When Working, say: "People work across functional boundaries without being directed to. 
Teams solve problems that belong to no single function because they own the enterprise outcome."

Add: "Information is shared proactively."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Silos are strong and quiet. 
Cross-functional problems stay unresolved because no one is accountable for the boundary."

Add: "Information is hoarded or filtered."

Ask: "Which problem in your organisation belongs to no single function today? Who is carrying it?"

3. Ownership Culture.
When Working, say: "Leaders and teams carry outcomes. 
When something goes wrong, people step in because they care about the result."

Add: "People step in without being required to. Accountability is cultural before it is structural."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "People complete tasks and declare them done, regardless of the downstream consequence. 
Accountability is assigned but not felt."

Add: "When something fails at a boundary, no one steps forward."

4. Strategic Alignment.
When Working, say: "Teams connect their day-to-day actions to the enterprise strategy without being reminded. 
When asked why they are doing something, they can trace it to the strategic intent."

Add: "Leaders can trace what they are doing to both the strategic intent and the SiP."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Teams are busy but unfocused. Actions are driven by habit or last year's priorities. 
The strategy exists in the boardroom but not on the floor."

Add: "Teams act on what the function has always done."

Ask: "When your teams are asked why they are doing something, can they trace it to the strategic intent?"

5. Dialogue Quality.
When Working, say: "Honest challenge, diverse perspective, and collective sense-making are normal. Disagreement surfaces before decisions are made."

Add: "Leaders can say they do not know something without losing credibility."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Meetings are performative. Consensus is assumed without being built. 
The most important concerns are raised only in corridors."

Add: "Fast, pattern-based thinking dominates and no deliberate, analytical thinking checks it."

Stay longest here. Honest challenge is the condition for an honest discussion of the other three indicators.

Ask: "Where are the most important concerns raised: in the meeting, or in the corridor afterwards?"

Deepen, say: "The strongest cultural signal is how people are treated in the corridor, how decisions are made when no one is watching, and whether the language of the email matches the language of the boardroom. 
If stated values show up only in formal settings, the culture has not yet landed. 
Work on the small interactions at the edges and the centre will follow."
(Insight: Values at the edges. Source: Journal, 18 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

6. Ask the room what it recognises.
Ask: "Which Signal of Absence in this domain do you recognise in your own organisation?"

Take two or three answers. Keep the discussion on what can be observed: what a customer, an employee or a board member would see or hear.

7. Link the domain to Section 5.
Say: "In Section 5 your group writes one People & Culture Dynamics statement. 
The lead question is: If the intent succeeds, what should be visible in how people understand, decide and behave? 
These indicators deepen that discussion. The statement itself stays focused on your own Strategy Intent."

8. Bridge to the next domain.
Say: "Next: D4, how the organisation benefits."

slides.title: 3.1e · D4 Enterprise Value
slides.notes:
3.1 — SiP OBSERVABLE INDICATORS · D4 · ENTERPRISE VALUE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Introduce the domain.
Say: "This domain is Enterprise Value Creation.
 It shows the commercial and strategic outcomes confirming the strategy is producing durable enterprise value."

2. Growth Trajectory.
When Working, say: "Revenue, market share, and customer acquisition are moving in the direction the strategic intent predicted. 
Growth is traceable to specific strategic choices."

Add: "Growth is deliberate."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Growth is inconsistent and driven by the market. 
The strategy does not explain the results."

Add: "Growth may be happening in arenas that were not part of the intended WHAT."

Ask: "Can you trace your growth to specific strategic choices, or does the market explain it?"

3. Profitability Quality.
When Working, say: "Margin discipline reflects deliberate value positioning. The organisation earns what its strategic intent says it should earn — its differentiation commands a premium."

Add: "The premium is earned because the organisation has chosen arenas where its differentiation commands it."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "Margin pressure is treated as a market problem when its root is positioning. 
The organisation competes on price because its WHY is insufficiently differentiated."

4. Market Position.
When Working, say: "The organisation occupies the competitive position its strategic intent described. 
Stakeholders describe the organisation in the language the SiP predicted."

Add: "The stakeholders in question are customers, partners, analysts and employees."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "The organisation's external reputation does not match its internal self-description. 
The strategy has not translated into a distinctive market position."

Add: "The strategy exists on paper only."

Ask: "Do stakeholders describe your organisation in the words you would use yourselves?"

5. Value Durability.
When Working, say: "The conditions that made success possible — talent, brand trust, infrastructure, ecosystem relationships, financial health — are being actively reinvested in and strengthened."

Add: "The organisation is building moats."

Signal of Absence, ask and listen for: "The organisation is harvesting value faster than it is creating it. 
Short-term results come at the cost of the capabilities that make future success possible."

Add: "Short-term results also cost the relationships that make future success possible."

Stay longest here. Value Durability is the SUSTAINS layer of the Value Triad, the layer most organisations under-invest in.

Ask: "Which condition of your future success are you reinvesting in least?"

Deepen, say: "Leaders who build structures to survive scarcity and crisis, and none to survive abundance and success, have protected against the wrong threat. Organisations that collapse in prosperity forget what made the prosperity possible."
(Insight: Surviving success. Source: Journal, 22 March 2026 — Professional Insights)

6. Ask the room what it recognises.
Ask: "Which Signal of Absence in this domain do you recognise in your own organisation?"
Take two or three answers. Keep the discussion on what can be observed: what a customer, an employee or a board member would see or hear.

7. Link the domain to Section 5.
Say: "In Section 5 your group writes one Enterprise Value Creation statement
. The lead question is: If the intent succeeds, how should the organisation benefit across its success metrics? These indicators deepen that discussion. The statement itself stays focused on your own Strategy Intent."

8. Bridge to 3.2.
Say: "We have looked at depth within each domain. Next we look at balance across all four."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write the 3.1 reflection: "From your assigned executive leader role: which SiP domain shows the most significant gaps in your organisation right now? What is the primary cause?"

slides.title: 3.2a · SiP Flammables: the balance test
slides.notes:
3.2 — SiP FLAMMABLES: WHEN THE PICTURE OF SUCCESS BECOMES DISTORTED (4 RISK PATTERNS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Start from one reality.
Say: "The four SiP domains are designed to describe one organisational reality."

2. Start from legitimacy.
Say: "In practice, leadership teams naturally bring different perspectives into the conversation. 
A commercial leader may see success primarily through customers and growth. 
An operations leader may emphasise efficiency, process and delivery. 
A people leader may focus on culture and capability. A finance leader may foreground financial and enterprise outcomes. 
Each perspective contributes something important."

Deepen, say: "A common diagnostic baseline matters. When the root condition is shared across the organisation, solutions built on the belief that one group is superior will fail."
(Insight: A common baseline. Source: Journal, 16 August 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

3. Name the risk.
Say: "The strategic risk emerges when one perspective becomes so dominant that it begins to define success for the entire organisation."

Deepen, say: "Whatever a team elevates above all else — speed, revenue, growth, reputation — will eventually be asked to deliver something it cannot. The test is whether the organisation has the honesty to see it when that happens."
(Insight: The single measure. Source: Journal, 23 January 2026 — Professional Insights: Culture)

4. Say what the Flammables are for.
Say: "This is what the SiP Flammables are designed to expose. They provide a balance test for the SiP. 
They help leaders recognise when a legitimate dimension of success has become disproportionately influential and the enterprise picture has started to narrow into a functional one."

Deepen, say: "The organisations most at risk are often the ones clearly succeeding on one or two dimensions while remaining unformed on the others. What is working reassures them that all is well, so they do not feel the cost of what is missing."
(Insight: Partial formation. Source: Journal, 26 March 2026 — Professional Insights)

5. Name the four patterns on the slide.

D1 Dominant — Customer Only: The SiP reads as a marketing aspiration.
At happens when other domains are not aligned:
The customer promise is made without accounting for the operational and cultural conditions required to deliver it. 
The organisation commits publicly to an experience it cannot yet produce at scale, so delivery teams absorb the gap through workarounds and overtime. 
Service becomes inconsistent, cost to serve rises faster than revenue, and the promise that was meant to differentiate the organisation becomes the source of customer disappointment.“

Ask: "Where would this risk show first in your organisation?"


D2 Dominant — Operations Only: The SiP reads as a process optimisation plan.
The organisation improves its machine while losing sight of what the machine is for. 
Execution becomes an end in itself. 
The efficiency gains are real, and the value they were meant to serve drifts: the organisation becomes faster at delivering what customers value less. People comply with the process without owning the outcome, so the system stops adapting when the market moves."

Ask: "Where would this risk show first in your organisation

D3 Dominant — People Only: The SiP reads as an organisational development narrative.
Culture work becomes disconnected from commercial outcomes. 
The strategy describes who the organisation wants to be and leaves what it intends to achieve undefined. 
Investment in people and culture cannot be defended when results come under pressure, so it is the first budget to be cut. 
Leaders outside the people function disengage from the SiP, and culture becomes one function's project."

Ask: "Where would this risk show first in your organisation?"

D4 Dominant — Value Only: The SiP reads as a financial target.
Say: "Leaders optimise for metrics without creating the conditions that produce them. 
Short-termism disguises itself as strategic clarity. 
Targets are met through cost cutting, price moves and deferred investment, which weakens the capabilities and relationships that future results depend on. 
Functions compete for the numbers they are measured on, and the enterprise outcome erodes while each scorecard stays green."

Ask: "Where would this risk show first in your organisation?"

6. Set the tone and bridge.
Say: "Every pattern grows from a legitimate perspective. We are here to see dominance early, while the SiP is still being written."

slides.title: Section 3 Reflection · Extrapolating
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 REFLECTION

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the question aloud.
Reflection — Extrapolating: "Based on the statement you made above, how would you describe Success in Practice for your organisation or team across its four domains?"

2. Say what the reflection is for.
Point learners to the portal section that they will be required to complete with as much depth as possible.
The reflections build the learning portfolio they receive at the end of the programme. Each one carries 20 of the 100 marks for the unit.

Say: "You write this reflection on the portal after the teaching, with as much depth as you can."

3. Set the standard.
Tell learners what a full answer does: Builds directly on their statement and describes success in observable terms across the four domains.

4. Say why naming the gap matters.
Say: "Honestly naming the gap between what has been achieved and what remains is the foundation of the next strategic phase. 
Organisations that settle for a vague awareness of more to do make little purposeful progress. Name the remaining work specifically, then plan for it."
(Insight: Naming the gap. Source: Journal, 10 April 2026 — Professional Insights: Strategy)

4. Bridge to Section 4.
Say: "We now have two tests for any Success in Practice: depth within each domain and balance across all four. 
Section 4 shows one company apply both tests to its Success in Practice. In Section 5 each group applies them to its own.""

Go back to the definitions participants wrote when the session opened.

The differences you noted on the chat. Ask two or three participants:

"Read your original definition of strategy. What would you change in it now — and why?"
Say: "The difference between your opening answer and your closing answer is the measure of what Unit 2 produced."

2. Read the five summary blocks aloud.

The summary is deliberately concise: its role is to crystallise the arc of the unit.

The blocks describe the whole unit, including the work the groups complete on the portal.

Awareness — What · What Was Established:
Strategy was defined precisely: the output of iterative thinking, logic and process to determine what, why, how and when an organisation creates, delivers and sustains value to its stakeholders while navigating the forces within its operating environment.
Each concept in the definition is part of the Strategy Architecture:

The Strategy Intent Statement brings forward four dimensions from that architecture (WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN) and crystallises them into one clear statement.

Success in Practice (SiP) defines what must be seen, experienced and executed for that ambition to become reality, across four observable domains: Customer Experience & Value, Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm, People & Culture Dynamics, and Enterprise Value Creation.

Intelligence — Why · Why It Matters:
The Strategy Intent and SiP become useful when they shape how the organisation aligns, makes choices and executes.

They serve three functions.
Strategic Alignment keeps people and functions oriented around the same ambition and picture of success.

The Decision Filter gives a basis for determining which choices, opportunities and investments support the strategy: the Strategy Intent tests strategic fit and SiP tests strategic contribution.

Execution Coherence helps functions understand how their individual contributions connect to produce the enterprise outcome.

Extrapolating — Where · Where Success Shows Up:
Each SiP domain was examined through observable indicators in two positions: When Working and Signal of Absence.
The indicators help leaders test, deepen and make observable the success they have defined.

Integration — Collective · What Was Shown:
One worked example took Kestrel Point Services through the three connected outputs.
Its Strategy Architecture: the integrated strategic logic constructed from the 14 elements, each stating what it is saying.
Its Strategy Intent Statement: the crisp expression of its ambition deduced from WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN.
Its Success in Practice: four statements describing what realising that ambition looks like across the organisation, tested for depth and balance.

Application — In Practice · What Was Built:
Each group built the same three outputs for its own simulated company. Every member agreed the group record, and the three outputs went into the team's Capstone S2R Blueprint.
The Architecture provides the logic. The Intent crystallises the ambition. Success in Practice makes the ambition observable.
These outputs are the strategic foundation that later S2R® work carries into alignment, execution and performance.


3. Run the tangible outputs check.
Before closing, confirm with the group that the following have been produced or are in progress:
- A Strategy Architecture from each group
- A Strategy Intent Statement from each group
- Four SiP statements from each group, agreed by every member

4. Ask for the closing commitment, on the slide.
Ask each participant to complete this sentence privately:
"Based on what Unit 2 revealed, the one thing I am committed to doing differently before our next session is…"
Post in the chat. These become the accountability anchors for Unit 3.

5. Give the transition to Unit 3.
Say: "What we built today is the strategic foundation: the Architecture, the Intent and the Success in Practice.

Unit 3 maps that Success in Practice and defines the Objectives and Key Results that will measure our progress towards it."

6. Hand over to the portal.
Say: "The teaching ends here. You now go to the portal and complete your own page, in the session or after it."
- Section 1: the opening definition of strategy and the 1.1 reflection.
- Section 2: the 2.1 reflection.
- Section 3: the 3.1 reflection.
- Section 4: the worked example, to read.
- Section 5, with the group: the Strategy Architecture, the Strategy Intent Statement and the four SiP statements of the group's simulated company. The group chooses its scribe for this work, the entries appear on every member's page, and each member selects Agree. Then the 5.1 reflection, on their own.
Participants then submit Unit 2 to the facilitator from their page.

AFTER THE SESSION:
- Review each participant’s reflections from the facilitator dashboard. The group's three outputs are Capstone work and are assessed independently at the capstone.
